segments.t: SSH tunnels securely forward traffic between local and remote ports through an encrypted SSH connection. korTTY supports three tunnel types: local port forwarding, remote port forwarding, and dynamic port forwarding (SOCKS proxy). They work like the KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002 options of OpenSSH and run over the login session of the terminal tab, so they need no second login.
Open a connection for editing: KTPH000Connections KTPH004 Manage ConnectionsKTPH001 → select the connection → KTPH002EditKTPH003.
Navigate to the KTPH000SSH TunnelsKTPH001 tab.
Click KTPH000AddKTPH001, choose the KTPH002TypeKTPH003 and fill in the fields. A new tunnel starts with KTPH004Enable tunnelKTPH005 ticked.

Click KTPH000SaveKTPH001 in the tunnel dialog, then KTPH002SaveKTPH003 in the connection editor. KTPH004CancelKTPH005 in the connection editor discards every tunnel you added, edited or removed since you opened it.
The tunnel dialog names its fields after the role they play for the chosen type and always lists the address that listens first, followed by the address the connections are forwarded to.
KTPH000Local bind addressKTPH001 and KTPH002Local portKTPH003 on your computer
KTPH000Remote bind addressKTPH001 and KTPH002Remote portKTPH003 on the SSH server
KTPH000Local bind addressKTPH001 and KTPH002Local portKTPH003 on your computer
KTPH000Remote hostKTPH001 and KTPH002Remote portKTPH003, as seen from the SSH server
KTPH000Local hostKTPH001 and KTPH002Local portKTPH003, as seen from your computer
Whatever destination the SOCKS client asks for

A bind address of KTPH000 (or leaving it empty) keeps the listener private to the computer it runs on. As soon as you enter another address, such as KTPH001 or a network interface, the dialog warns that other computers can reach the tunnel; for a remote tunnel the warning adds that the SSH server only accepts such an address when its KTPH002 setting allows it.
Multiple tunnels can be configured per connection. Disabled tunnels remain in the configuration but are not opened when the connection connects.

The KTPH007SSH TunnelsKTPH008 tab lists every tunnel the way KTPH000 options read, listener first: KTPH001, KTPH002 or KTPH003, followed by its description. KTPH004 marks an enabled tunnel and KTPH005 a disabled one. A tunnel that other computers may reach is marked as such in the list, so a forgotten KTPH006 stands out.

KTPH000Enable SSH tunnelsKTPH001 above the list switches every tunnel of the connection on or off at once. It is ticked when all tunnels are enabled and shows a dash when only some are; clicking the dash enables all of them. Switching a single tunnel is done with KTPH002Enable tunnelKTPH003 in its own dialog.
Forward a local port to a remote service through the SSH tunnel.
KTPH000Example use case:KTPH001 Access a remote database server that is not directly reachable from your machine.
Once connected, connect to the remote database using KTPH000 on your machine.
Make a local service accessible on the SSH server.
KTPH000Example use case:KTPH001 Let a program on the SSH server reach a development server on your machine.
KTPH001Remote bind address:KTPH002 KTPH000 (the address the SSH server listens on)
KTPH001Remote port:KTPH002 KTPH000 (the port the SSH server listens on)
KTPH001Local host:KTPH002 KTPH000 (where your computer forwards each connection)

After connecting, programs on the SSH server reach your service at KTPH000. Like OpenSSH, korTTY asks the server to listen on its loopback address only. Setting KTPH005Remote bind addressKTPH006 to KTPH001 asks the server to accept connections from its network as well; an OpenSSH server only does that when its KTPH002 setting is KTPH003, and korTTY marks such a tunnel in the tunnel dialog, the tunnel list and the status bar as reachable from other computers. A server with KTPH004 listens on all its addresses for every remote tunnel, whatever bind address you enter.
Create a SOCKS proxy for network traffic through the SSH tunnel.
KTPH000Example use case:KTPH001 Encrypt all traffic from your browser or application by routing it through the SSH tunnel.
KTPH001Local port:KTPH002 KTPH000 (or any available port)
Configure your browser or application to use KTPH000 as a SOCKS5 (or SOCKS4) proxy. Host names are resolved by the SSH server.
A dynamic tunnel only uses the local bind address and the local port; the remote fields are disabled for this type.

KTPH000Once per terminal tab:KTPH001 the tunnels open right after login on the tab's first SSH session and stay open while the tab is connected. Split panes neither open them again nor conflict with them.

KTPH000Asked once:KTPH001 the first time a connection's tunnels are about to open, korTTY lists them and asks KTPH002Open TunnelsKTPH003 or KTPH004Not NowKTPH005. KTPH006Not NowKTPH007 is the default button, so a key you are still typing into the terminal when the question appears never opens them. The answer is remembered for that connection; korTTY asks again when its tunnels or its server change. KTPH008Not NowKTPH009 applies to the tab, including its reconnects — open the connection in a new tab to be asked again.
KTPH000Reconnect:KTPH001 a manual or automatic reconnect closes the tunnels first and opens them again on the new session.

KTPH001Closing panes:KTPH002 if you close the pane the tunnels run on (or type KTPH000 there) while a pane opened with KTPH003Split Right (same server)KTPH004 or KTPH005Split Down (same server)KTPH006 from a pane on the tab's server stays open, the tunnels move to that pane. Panes opened with KTPH007Split Right (new connection)KTPH008 or KTPH009Split Down (new connection)KTPH010, and the same-server splits made from them, never take them over, even when they connect to the same server.
KTPH000Closing the tabKTPH001 closes its tunnels.

KTPH000Two tabs, one connection:KTPH001 each tab opens its own tunnels, so in the second tab a local or dynamic tunnel reports that the address is already in use, and a remote tunnel that the SSH server refused it. The first tab keeps working.
KTPH000Not openedKTPH001 by SFTP tabs, by Mosh connections (the status bar says that tunnels need the SSH protocol), or for splits to a different server.

KTPH001Server side:KTPH002 the SSH server must allow forwarding (KTPH000 in OpenSSH). A remote tunnel the server refuses (forwarding disabled, or its port already in use on the server) is reported in the status bar; the other tunnels still open.

While a tab has tunnels, its status bar shows KTPH000, followed by the first tunnel that failed and why (for example KTPH001) and by the first tunnel that other computers may reach. Hover over the status bar to see every tunnel with its state.
Tunnels of a connection that comes from a KTPH000TeamworkKTPH001 source were written by whoever edits the shared file, so korTTY limits them:
Remote tunnels are never opened, whatever address they name: loopback on a shared SSH server is reachable by every account on it.
Local and dynamic tunnels may only listen on KTPH000.
The rest still needs your one-time confirmation, which points out that the tunnels come from the shared file.
To use a different tunnel, create your own connection to the same server and add the tunnel there; shared connections cannot be duplicated in the connection manager.
An administrator can forbid all tunnels with KTPH000 in the KTPH001enterprise policyKTPH002. The status bar then says that tunnels are disabled by your organization.

KTPH000Enable/Disable:KTPH001 toggle KTPH002Enable tunnelKTPH003 on a tunnel, or KTPH004Enable SSH tunnelsKTPH005 for all of them, to activate or deactivate tunnels without removing the configuration.
KTPH000Edit:KTPH001 select a tunnel and click KTPH002EditKTPH003 to change its settings.
KTPH000Remove:KTPH001 select a tunnel and click KTPH002RemoveKTPH003 to delete it from the connection.
KTPH000Multiple tunnels:KTPH001 any number of tunnels can be configured on a single connection and opened together.

Saving the connection applies the change to every open tab of that connection right away: switched-off or removed tunnels close, and a changed set of tunnels replaces the running one on the same session — after the one-time question unless you already allowed exactly that set. A tab whose tunnels did not change keeps them open, so editing only a description or another setting of the connection does not interrupt them. A tab that is disconnected or still logging in at that moment opens the saved tunnels once it is connected.

Tunnels imported from PuTTY Connection Manager keep their type, ports and target host. The CSV format names no bind address, so korTTY binds every imported listener to KTPH000, which is also PuTTY's default for remote tunnels. Remote tunnels that earlier versions imported were stored with the remote bind address KTPH001; the tunnel list, the tunnel dialog and the status bar mark them as reachable from other computers, so set their KTPH003Remote bind addressKTPH004 to KTPH002 if the forwarded port should stay private to the server.

Ports below 1024 (such as 80 or 443) need elevated privileges: on your computer for local and dynamic tunnels, and a root login on the SSH server for remote tunnels. Use ports 1024 and above to avoid permission issues.
